caveats: **`health` is the drive's own critical-warning flag, and only Windows NVMe drives have one.** Wear and spare percentages never feed the verdict, so a heavily worn drive with no warning flag reads `ok`. SATA, USB and virtual machine disks report `unknown` because `IOCTL_STORAGE_PREDICT_FAILURE` is deliberately not used as a fallback (it fails on NVMe), so a missing `failing` is not evidence of a healthy drive.

**macOS reports identity only.** `health` is always `unknown` and `pct_used` and `spare_pct` are always `-`, because the attributes sit behind Apple's private `IONVMeSMARTUserClient` interface, which the plugin does not use; every macOS `smart` run is also `CONSTRAINED` with `macos:iokit:health_unread`.

**Linux is declared, not implemented.** Both actions return one placeholder row (`health=unsupported`, or `volume=-`) and `UNAVAILABLE`, and the definitions target Windows and macOS only. A Linux leg would bind the NVMe admin get-log-page call, whose log page the Windows decoder already reads, and has not been measured on real storage. `topology` is advertised `planned` on all three OSes (and `partitions` on Linux and macOS), though Windows has no LVM/md topology source and macOS has no multipath; the leg PRs move such legs to a typed `unsupported` with a reason, so until then `<os>:planned` means "not read", never "this host has no partitions".

**No deadline on Windows device I/O.** `DeviceIoControl` is synchronous with no timeout, so a wedged device or a disconnected network LUN can park the dispatch worker that called it. The 64-drive probe limit and suppression of the not-ready-volume dialog bound the ordinary case, not a driver that never returns.

**Windows `partitions` is what `Win32_DiskPartition` exposes, not a byte-exact map of the disk.** It omits the 16 MiB Microsoft Reserved partition (measured: three partitions where `MSFT_Partition` shows four), and `mount_points` are drive letters only, so a folder mount or a letterless volume shows `-` (`volumes` reports those). Measured on one bare-metal GPT host with a second GPT disk; unmeasured: dynamic disks, BitLocker-locked volumes, Storage Spaces and non-English `Type` strings. A local fixed drive letter the association cannot place reads `constrained` (`unplaced_volume`), never "no mount point": find the letter with `volumes`, and expect RAM disks, encrypted-container mounts and virtual drives. `disk` is `PhysicalDrive<N>`, as in `smart` and `volumes`, not the device record's integer `idx`. For a `wmi_*` or `no_rows` reason, `winmgmt /verifyrepository` (as administrator) checks the repository.

definitions.description: Reports the partitions of each physical disk with size, partition type and mount points. Read on Windows (Win32_DiskPartition with the drive letters from Win32_LogicalDiskToPartition; the 16 MiB Microsoft Reserved partition is not listed by that class, and a folder mount point shows no mount point). Not read yet on Linux or macOS: a dispatch there answers one unsupported status row (linux:planned or macos:planned) until its leg lands. It is dispatched by the daily device-record sync, so its status is recorded as the partition section of the record.

Reports per-physical-drive health: model, transport, media type and, where the operating system exposes them, wear indicators. On Windows the wear, available-spare and critical-warning figures are read from the NVMe SMART/Health log, so an NVMe drive reports them and a SATA or USB drive reports identity and media type with health "unknown" rather than a guess — IOCTL_STORAGE_PREDICT_FAILURE is deliberately not used as a substitute because it fails on NVMe. On macOS the leg reports identity and whether the device advertises NVMe SMART, but NOT the health attributes: those are reachable only through a private, undocumented Apple interface, so health reports "unknown" there on every device. The Linux leg is not implemented in this release and says so. Three columns carry FIXED vocabularies, emitted verbatim and safe to group or alert on. health: ok, warning, failing, unknown (the device did not tell us), unsupported (this OS leg cannot ask — every Linux row today). bus: nvme, sata, usb, sas, virtual, unknown. media: ssd, hdd, unknown. A value outside these sets is never emitted.

Reports the logical storage layers above the physical disks: LVM volume groups and logical volumes, md arrays, multipath maps and APFS containers. Not read yet on any OS: every dispatch answers one unsupported status row (windows:planned, linux:planned or macos:planned) until its leg lands; Windows has no source ruled yet and stays planned. It is dispatched by the daily device-record sync, so its status (including the planned one) is recorded as the topology section of the record.

Reports which physical drive backs which logical volume and mount point. This is deliberately not a general volume inventory — `hardware.disks` already lists physical devices and `crossplatform.storage.mounts` already lists mounts; this action carries the join between them, so a failing drive can be named in terms of the volumes it serves. On Windows a volume spanning several drives reports every drive it touches, and a volume with no drive letter or mount point reports "-" for mount points rather than being omitted. On macOS the physical drive is resolved by walking the IOKit provider chain, so an APFS volume on a synthesized container correctly reports the underlying physical disk rather than the container. The Linux leg is not implemented in this release. total_bytes here is RAW MEDIA CAPACITY, not filesystem capacity, and it is NOT comparable with crossplatform.storage.mounts.total_bytes: on Windows it is the sum of the volume's disk extents, on macOS the IOMedia size, while the mounts action reports the filesystem's own total. fstype and total_bytes are carried only to identify the volume in the join; for capacity reporting use crossplatform.storage.mounts or crossplatform.storage.free.

description: Reports physical drive health and the mapping between drives and the logical volumes they back
how_it_works:
Both actions are reads and change nothing. `smart` lists the physical drives the OS exposes and reports each one's model, transport (`bus`) and media type; on Windows, NVMe drives also answer a SMART/Health query whose critical-warning flags become a `health` verdict, with the raw wear and spare-capacity percentages alongside. `volumes` lists logical volumes and, for each, the physical drive that backs it and the mount points or drive letters it serves. On Windows `smart` probes `PhysicalDrive0` to `PhysicalDrive63`; on macOS both actions walk the IOKit registry; Linux returns a single placeholder row and an `UNAVAILABLE` status.

`volumes` is deliberately not a third volume inventory: `hardware.disks` already lists physical devices and `filesystem_posture.mounts` already lists mounts. This action carries only the join between them, which is what lets a failing-drive alert name the drive letters or mount points it affects. Where a mechanism is unavailable (Linux) or is reachable only through a private OS interface (macOS health), the leg says so in its result rather than guessing.

`partitions` is read on Windows: one row per partition `Win32_DiskPartition` reports, with the drive letters `Win32_LogicalDiskToPartition` maps to it, through the bounded WMI helper (`agents/shared/wmi_bounded.hpp`), plus a `Win32_LogicalDisk` cross-check; each call has a deadline, but the connect step keeps WMI's own max-wait, so the read is bounded, not instantaneous. Everywhere else `partitions`, and `topology` on every OS, read nothing yet: each answers with exactly one `status|<action>|unsupported|<os>:planned` row from the shared planned-leg reporter (`agents/shared/planned_leg.hpp`), until its leg PR lands (partitions on Linux and macOS; topology on Linux for LVM/md/multipath and on macOS for APFS containers; Windows has no topology source ruled yet).

### What you can decide with it

| Question | Action and column | Windows | macOS | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Is a drive reporting a failure or warning? | `smart` `health` | `failing` or `warning` for NVMe drives only (derivation below) | Never; `health` is always `unknown` | Nothing |
| How worn is the drive? | `smart` `pct_used`, `spare_pct` | NVMe drives only. `pct_used` runs 0 to 255 and can exceed 100 | `-` | Nothing |
| What kind of drive is it? | `smart` `model`, `bus`, `media` | All drives the OS lists | All block devices, disk images included (`bus` `virtual`) | Nothing |
| Which drive letters or mount points does this drive serve? | `volumes` `device`, `mount_points` | One row per volume; a spanned volume lists one entry per disk extent, comma-separated, so the same drive can appear more than once | One row per partition or container member that maps a mount or a drive; `device` is the physical disk, for example `disk0` | Nothing |
| How full is it, or what is its filesystem usage? | not this plugin | Use `crossplatform.storage.mounts` | Use `crossplatform.storage.mounts` | n/a |

How `health` is derived. For an NVMe drive the plugin reads the SMART/Health log page and looks only at its critical-warning byte. If bit 0 (available spare below threshold) or bit 2 (reliability degraded) is set, `health` is `failing`. If any other bit is set (temperature, media read-only, volatile-memory backup failed, or a bit the plugin does not know), it is `warning`. If no bit is set it is `ok`. `pct_used` and `spare_pct` are reported but never change the verdict, so a drive at 100 percent or more of its rated endurance with no warning flag still reads `ok`; set your own wear threshold on `pct_used` if you want one.

What a missing `failing` does and does not prove. Only Windows NVMe drives are ever judged. SATA and USB drives, virtual machine disks and every drive on macOS report `unknown`, and Linux reports `unsupported`, so the absence of a `failing` row says nothing about those devices. Alert on `failing` and `warning`, and track the `unknown` and `unsupported` rows separately to see which devices the fleet cannot judge. `ok` means the drive reported no critical warning at read time, not that it will not fail.

### Diagrams

#### From a drive to a `health` value

Wear (`pct_used`) and spare (`spare_pct`) come from the same log page and are printed on the row, but the decision uses the critical-warning byte alone. Every path that cannot read the page ends in `unknown`, never in `ok`.

#### How `volumes` joins volumes to drives

On Windows the physical drive comes from the volume's disk extents, so a spanned or striped volume names every drive it touches. On macOS the drive comes from walking the IOKit provider chain, because trimming the BSD name would stop at a synthesized APFS container that is not a physical device. A whole disk that serves no mount point is left out, since it carries no join.

outputs_note: Pipe-delimited rows, one per drive, volume or partition. Field 0 is a literal discriminator (`smart` or `volume`; `partitions` on Windows answers one `status|partitions|<level>|<tokens>` row first, then its `partition` rows; the planned actions answer one `status` row, `status|<action>|unsupported|<os>:planned`, and the `topology` row schema is declared in `disk_actions_legs.hpp`) that precedes the columns below; every row of a kind has the same field count, with `-` where a value is inapplicable or was not read. `-` never means zero, and a macOS `smart` row always has `-` for `pct_used` and `spare_pct`. Every free-text field (device, model, volume, mount points, filesystem, detail) passes through `safe_output_field`, which rewrites `\` as `/`; `bus`, `media` and `health` are fixed vocabularies and the numeric fields are digits, so they need no escaping. Windows volume GUID paths read `//?/Volume{…}/` and drive letters `C:/`. A leg that finds nothing still emits one placeholder row so zero rows can never be misread as "no disks": a `smart` placeholder carries `health=unsupported`, a `volume` placeholder carries `volume=-`, and both are accompanied by a typed status, which is the authoritative signal. `total_bytes` is media capacity, not filesystem capacity: on macOS every APFS volume in a container reports the container's size, and unmounted members and containers appear with `-` mount points; on Windows it is the sum of the volume's disk extents. Use `crossplatform.storage.mounts` for real capacity.

Every macOS `smart` run reports `macos:iokit:health_unread` (identity read, health not) unless a stronger cause outranks it. `windows:physicaldrive_cap` means the probe of `PhysicalDrive0` to `PhysicalDrive63` did not end in a run of eight absent indices, so a host with more drives may be reported short. `windows:volume_extents:truncated` means a volume reported more disk extents than the reply could carry, so its `device` lists only some drives

stamp.privilege: NT SERVICE virtual service account (not an administrator)

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result only.** Rows travel over the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response, land in the ResponseStore (90-day default retention), and are queryable at `/api/responses/{id}`, aggregatable (`smart` by `health`, `volumes` by `device`) and exportable as JSON from `/api/responses/{id}/export`.

**Daily-sync consumer for three of the four actions.** The `device_ci` daily-sync source (ADR-0016) invokes `volumes`, `partitions` and `topology` in-process via `LocalDispatcher` on every cycle and reports them as the `volume`, `partition` and `topology` sections of its device record, each with its own status, so a planned leg's `unsupported` status (`<os>:planned`) is recorded even though it has no rows. `smart` is not part of that record. A host without this plugin reports the three sections as unavailable (`agent:plugin_not_loaded`). On Windows the daily sync does not invoke `volumes` (its `DeviceIoControl` calls have no deadline, and the sync thread is joined on reconnect and on shutdown), so the Windows `volume` section reads `unavailable` with `agent:windows_volumes_unbounded` until plugin OS calls have a deadline (#3925); the operator-triggered action is unchanged.
**Not consumed by** the Echo warehouse, DEX, or metrics. Nothing else runs on a schedule.

**Sensitivity.** Rows identify hardware, not people: drive models, volume GUIDs and BSD names are device-level identifiers (asset-inventory class, like `device_ci`), and nothing in them names a user, a file or an application, with one exception: a mount-point entry reports the path the OS gave, so a volume folder-mounted under a user profile, or an APFS volume mounted at `/Volumes/<label>`, can name an account or carry a personal label. The `device_ci` daily-sync consumer replaces such entries with `[redacted]` before it sends them and marks the section `constrained` (`agent:mount_points_redacted`); a direct `volumes` or `partitions` dispatch returns them unchanged.

**MCP / REST.** Discover: `discover_plugins` (summary) → `yuzu://plugin-docs` (this page as data) → `discover_instructions` / `get_definition("crossplatform.storage.smart")`. Run: `execute_instruction {definition_id, parameters}`. Read: `/api/responses/{id}`.
